title: 2. What the ETF Holds: Sub-Industry Segments, Weighting Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Inside the 54-Stock Vault: Five Insurance Business Models and How Money Actually Flows

epigraph.quote: An insurance broker sells umbrellas without ever paying for the rain; a catastrophe reinsurer sells the ark and prays the flood stays below the attachment point.
epigraph.author: Specialty Insurance Market Desk

web_blocks.html: Broad Financials funds are dominated by money-center banks and payment networks. By contrast, KIE is a 100% pure-play U.S. insurance portfolio holding 54 equity constituents as of November 23, 2026 [1]. Under S&P Dow Jones Indices' GICS rules, the S&P Insurance Select Industry Index draws from five sub-industries inside the S&P Total Market Index [1][3]. Those sleeves are Property & Casualty (56.29%), Life & Health (19.89%), Insurance Brokers (14.05%), Reinsurance (7.88%), and Multi-Line (1.89%) [1][3]. KIE uses modified equal weighting (~1.85% initial weight per stock at each quarterly rebalance). As a result, each sleeve's weight tracks the number of listed companies in that group rather than mega-cap market value [1][2].

web_blocks.takeaway: Equal weighting puts mid-cap specialty insurers and wholesale brokers on equal footing with $141 billion giants. Every stock starts near the same ~2% portfolio weight [1].

web_blocks.html: 1. Property & Casualty Insurance (56.29% weight) — Concrete Real-World Example: Consider how The Progressive Corporation runs U.S. personal auto, a $211 billion industry line in 2025 direct premiums [16]. A household in Ohio or Texas buys a six-month policy online or through an independent agent and pays upfront. That upfront cash creates immediate float [16]. Progressive uses Snapshot telematics and actuarial pricing to segment risk across 40.5 million policies in force as of October 2026 [16]. After a collision, adjusters pay repair and medical bills out of loss reserves. Any premium left after claims and operating costs becomes underwriting profit [16]. In December 2025, Progressive posted an 87.1% combined ratio, keeping $12.90 of underwriting profit per $100 of earned premium. Rising competition later nudged its October 2026 combined ratio to 91.2% [16]. Top-10 specialty P&C holdings—Palomar Holdings (2.20%), RLI Corp. (2.06%), and Skyward Specialty (2.05%)—apply this short-tail model to earthquake, surety, and E&S niches [1].

2. Life & Health Insurance (19.89% weight) — Concrete Real-World Example: Unlike annual P&C policies, life and annuity carriers make multi-decade promises [15]. Picture a 62-year-old retiree buying a Fixed Indexed Annuity (FIA) or Registered Index-Linked Annuity (RILA) from Prudential Financial, MetLife, or Corebridge. U.S. retail annuity sales hit $434.1 billion in 2024 and $223 billion in 1H 2025 (+3% YoY) [15]. RILAs surged over 270% from $24 billion in 2020 to $65 billion in 2024, with over $75 billion projected for 2025–2026 [15]. The carrier invests the lump-sum deposit in corporate bonds, private placements, and structured credit yielding ~5.0%–5.5%. It credits the buyer a lower guaranteed or hedged rate and pockets the spread over 7 to 20 years [15]. Meanwhile, supplemental carrier Aflac collects payroll-deducted premiums in the U.S. and Japan. In Q2 2026, Aflac hit a 92.7% Japan persistency rate, a 20.9% U.S. pretax margin, and repositioned $4.8 billion of bonds to boost investment income [15].

3. Insurance Brokers (14.05% weight) — Concrete Real-World Example: Insurance brokers are the highest-return, lowest-capital toll bridges inside KIE [14][17]. Key holdings include Ryan Specialty Holdings (2.13% weight, #2 holding) and Marsh & McLennan (2.08% weight, #4 holding) [1]. Suppose a coastal Florida resort or national trucking fleet cannot get standard coverage due to hurricane or nuclear-verdict risk. The client's retail broker calls Ryan Specialty, a wholesale intermediary, which builds a layered Excess & Surplus (E&S) policy across multiple underwriters [17]. Ryan Specialty takes zero underwriting balance-sheet risk. It earns a commission on bound premiums and posted a 30.9% Adjusted EBITDAC margin on $790.0 million of Q3 2026 revenue [17]. Still, broker commissions scale directly with policy pricing. When commercial property rates softened, Ryan Specialty's organic revenue growth cooled from 15.0% in Q3 2025 to 4.0% in Q3 2026 [17].

4. Reinsurance (7.88% weight) — Concrete Real-World Example: Reinsurers act as the insurers' insurers [14][18]. KIE holds Everest Group (2.05% weight) and RenaissanceRe (RNR) [1][18]. A regional U.S. homeowners carrier wants to protect its surplus against a 1-in-50-year hurricane or wildfire. It buys a catastrophe excess-of-loss treaty from RenaissanceRe, paying an upfront premium so RenaissanceRe absorbs losses above a set attachment point [18]. In Q3 2026, RenaissanceRe posted a strong 79.7% overall combined ratio. It also earned $440.9 million in net investment income (5.8% yield to maturity) and $81.7 million in third-party capital fees [18]. Yet that same quarter showed reinsurance's twin risks. Casualty & Specialty combined ratio jumped to 110.6% (including 10.5 points from 2026 Large Loss Events like Middle East conflict losses). At the same time, rising yields drove $879.8 million in mark-to-market bond losses and a -$161.4 million GAAP net loss despite $512.6 million in operating income [18].

5. Multi-Line Insurance (1.89% weight) — Concrete Real-World Example: Multi-line carriers blend distinct risk pools under one roof [14][19]. Kemper Corporation (2.09% weight, #3 holding) pairs non-standard personal auto P&C with a steady life insurance unit [1][19]. After repair inflation hit specialty auto, management tightened standards and exited weak states. Policies in force fell 8.3% sequentially to 1.006 million in Q3 2026, lifting its Specialty P&C combined ratio by 4.8 points to 99.2% on $858 million of earned premiums [19]. CEO Steve McAnena noted on the Q3 2026 call: "We'll take them one at a time, beginning with profitability, because it's foundational to everything we do" [19]. Alongside Kemper, Assurant (2.02% weight) pairs mobile-device protection with lender-placed homeowners coverage. This shows how KIE's equal-weight basket captures hybrid fee-and-underwriting models [1].

book_paragraphs: When you open the hood of KIE, the first thing that strikes you is how clean and unpolluted the exposure is. Many investors assume that buying a broad Financials ETF gives them insurance exposure, only to discover that big banks, payment networks, and asset managers crowd out the underwriters. KIE, by contrast, is a 100% pure-play insurance vault holding 54 U.S.-listed equities across five distinct GICS sub-industries: Property & Casualty Insurance at 56.29%, Life & Health Insurance at 19.89%, Insurance Brokers at 14.05%, Reinsurance at 7.88%, and Multi-Line Insurance at 1.89%. Because every stock starts near an equal 1.85% weight at each quarterly rebalance, the largest constituent in KIE as of late November 2026 isn't a $140 billion juggernaut—it's Palomar Holdings, a mid-cap specialty earthquake and property insurer, sitting at 2.20%.

To truly understand what you own when you buy KIE, let's walk through all five business models using concrete, real-world transactions—because each sub-industry earns its keep in a completely different way.

Start with the engine room: Property & Casualty Insurance, which makes up more than half the fund. Imagine a family in Columbus, Ohio buying a six-month personal auto policy from The Progressive Corporation. They pay premiums upfront, giving Progressive immediate cash float across 40.5 million policies in force. Progressive uses driving telematics and rapid pricing updates to keep its combined ratio well below 100%—delivering an 87.1% combined ratio in December 2025 before competition nudged it to 91.2% in October 2026. Every dollar below 100 cents on the dollar is pure underwriting profit, and Progressive invests the float in Treasuries and investment-grade bonds while waiting to pay collision claims. Right alongside Progressive in KIE sit nimble specialty P&C underwriters like Palomar, RLI, and Skyward Specialty, insuring everything from California earthquakes to commercial surety bonds.

Now move to the second pillar: Life & Health Insurance, at nearly 20% of the fund. Here, the time horizon stretches from six months to twenty years. Picture a 62-year-old engineer rolling over retirement savings into a Fixed Indexed Annuity or a Registered Index-Linked Annuity issued by Prudential Financial, MetLife, or Corebridge. Industry-wide U.S. retail annuity sales hit $434.1 billion in 2024 and $223 billion in the first half of 2025, with RILAs exploding from $24 billion in 2020 to over $75 billion projected for 2025 and 2026. The life insurer invests that long-term deposit in corporate bonds, private credit, and structured securities earning over 5%, credits a lower return to the retiree, and pockets the spread. It is a spread-lending business dressed in actuarial clothes—wonderful when interest rates sit at 4% to 5%, and treacherous if credit defaults spike or interest rates plunge back toward zero.

Third, look at KIE's quiet crown jewel: Insurance Brokers, at 14.05% of the fund. Companies like Marsh & McLennan, Aon, Arthur J. Gallagher, Brown & Brown, and Ryan Specialty do not pay a single hurricane claim or jury verdict. When a coastal hotel chain needs complex Excess & Surplus property coverage, a wholesale broker like Ryan Specialty places the policy with underwriters and collects a recurring commission. In Q3 2026, Ryan Specialty generated $790 million in revenue at a 30.9% Adjusted EBITDAC margin with almost no balance-sheet risk. The catch? Because commissions are a percentage of premiums, falling commercial property rates immediately slow broker growth—which is why Ryan Specialty's organic growth cooled from 15.0% a year earlier to 4.0% in Q3 2026.

Fourth comes Reinsurance, at 7.88% of KIE—the wholesale shock absorber of global finance. When a primary insurer wants to cap its hurricane or wildfire exposure, it buys a catastrophe treaty from Everest Group or RenaissanceRe. In Q3 2026, RenaissanceRe posted a razor-sharp 79.7% overall combined ratio, earned $440.9 million in net investment income at a 5.8% yield to maturity, and collected $81.7 million in third-party capital fees. Yet that very same quarter reminded investors why reinsurers trade at volatile multiples: large geopolitical and specialty losses pushed RenaissanceRe's Casualty & Specialty combined ratio to 110.6%, while rising bond yields created $879.8 million in mark-to-market bond losses and a GAAP net loss of $161.4 million.

Finally, Multi-Line Insurance—at 1.89%—represents hybrid platforms like Kemper and Assurant that combine P&C underwriting with life insurance or device-protection fee streams. Kemper's recent turnaround captures the brutal discipline required in insurance: management intentionally shrank its specialty auto policy count by 8.3% in a single quarter to shed unprofitable drivers, lifting its Specialty P&C combined ratio by nearly five full points to 99.2%. As CEO Steve McAnena told investors, 'We'll take them one at a time, beginning with profitability, because it's foundational to everything we do.' Put all five sub-industries together, and you see why KIE is far more balanced—and far more nuanced—than a single-stock bet on any one insurer.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Notice how KIE's equal-weight design quietly reshapes your sector exposure. In a cap-weighted insurance fund, Progressive and Chubb alone can consume over a quarter of your money. In KIE, a wholesale E&S broker like Ryan Specialty, a specialty earthquake writer like Palomar, and a turnaround auto insurer like Kemper each carry roughly 2% of your capital—giving you a true cross-section of the entire U.S. risk-transfer ecosystem.

section_takeaway: KIE blends five distinct insurance economic models—P&C (56.29%), Life & Health (19.89%), capital-light Brokers (14.05%), Reinsurance (7.88%), and Multi-Line (1.89%)—at ~1.85% equal weights, trading mega-cap concentration for full-ecosystem breadth [1].

book_subsections.title: How Float, Commissions, and Treaties Interact Inside One Ticker
paragraphs: One of the most rewarding exercises you and I can do with KIE is compare how cash enters the door across its three largest sub-industries. When Progressive collects a six-month personal auto premium, that cash sits on its balance sheet as unearned premium and loss reserves—float that earns bond interest until a collision claim is settled. When Prudential or MetLife collects an annuity deposit, that float stretches out for ten to twenty years, making investment spread management and credit underwriting the entire ballgame.

Now contrast both of those balance-sheet businesses with Marsh & McLennan, Aon, Arthur J. Gallagher, Brown & Brown, and Ryan Specialty inside KIE's 14.05% Insurance Brokers sleeve. Brokers hold virtually no underwriting reserves and never write a check for a hurricane roof claim or a trucking verdict. Their economics resemble toll roads on global risk transfer: as long as commercial insured values rise and complex risks migrate into the Excess & Surplus market, brokers clip a high-margin commission on every policy placed. Pairing 85.95% balance-sheet risk-takers with 14.05% capital-light toll bridges gives KIE an internal stabilizer that pure P&C funds simply do not possess.

Step back and appreciate the portfolio-level consequence of holding all five sub-industries inside one ticker. When commercial property pricing cools, property-catastrophe reinsurers and specialty writers feel the pinch first, while personal auto insurers like Progressive follow their own repair-cost and telematics cycle and life insurers like Prudential and MetLife trade primarily on intermediate Treasury yields and credit spreads. Meanwhile, fee-based brokers like Marsh & McLennan and Ryan Specialty keep collecting recurring commissions without putting a single dollar of statutory surplus on the line against a hurricane. KIE’s five-cylinder engine rarely fires on every cylinder at once—and rarely stalls on all five simultaneously.
